problem: Prior social navigation work either relies on hand-designed pedestrian models (e.g., social force) that miss real interaction complexity, or on robot datasets that are small and expensive to collect. Existing datasets are teleoperated (JRDB, SCAND), scripted or non-visual (THÖR, CoBoT), or contain no robot at all (MuSoHu). None of them supports learning an RGB-only visual navigation policy that avoids disturbing people.
motivation: Robots that share spaces with people should not change how humans would naturally move. That requires a predictive model of human behavior conditioned on robot actions, and such a model in turn needs large amounts of real human-robot interaction data. The authors define 'socially unobtrusive' as minimal counterfactual perturbation: would the human have walked the same way if the robot had stopped and given way? They also build an autonomous, interaction-seeking data collection system so that scaling the data becomes cheap.
key_idea: Train an end-to-end RGB image-goal navigation policy with a differentiable cost. The cost penalizes the difference between a learned pedestrian predictor's forecast under the robot's planned trajectory and its forecast under a stationary 'give-way' robot, plus a personal-space term. The predictor is trained on a large, autonomously collected, interaction-enriched human-robot dataset (HuRoN).
insight: The quality of the counterfactual objective depends on the accuracy of the human-dynamics model, and that accuracy depends on the training data containing close human-robot interactions. On data from the interaction-seeking collection policy, predictor MSE drops to 0.0084 (vs 0.0099 on naïve data and 0.0147 with social-force simulation only), and closed-loop SACSoN reaches GR 1.000 with 1 pedestrian collision. The same objective trained on the naïve subset gives GR 0.667 and 8 collisions, which is worse than ExAug's GR 0.800. So an inaccurate predictor yields a conservative policy that stalls or still collides, and the proposed losses only pay off with interaction-rich data. Mixing social-force simulated trajectories into real batches gives a small further gain (0.0083 MSE, 0.876 cosine).
method: Base visual navigation (from ExAug): topological graph of goal images, built from a teleoperated traversal subsampled at 0.5 fps. An 8-layer CNN policy maps the current image, 5 past frames and a subgoal image to Ns=8 future (v, ω) commands; only the first command is executed (receding horizon). It is trained without imitation by minimizing a differentiable geometric cost J_nav = J_pose + w_c·J_col + w_r·J_reg.

Pedestrian dynamics model f_ψ: an MLP that predicts the future 2D pedestrian trajectory from the past human trajectory, the past robot trajectory (odometry) and the robot's future trajectory, all in robot coordinates. Human tracks come from YOLOv5 + DeepSORT on spherical panoramas, projected to 3D with ExAug depth/scale estimates. It is pre-trained with MSE, with half of each batch from 10,000 social-force-simulated scenarios, then frozen.

Counterfactual perturbation loss J_cp: the mean squared difference between f_ψ's prediction when the robot's future trajectory is a zero vector (stopping to give way) and its prediction under the trajectory integrated from the policy's velocities. Gradients back-propagate through the frozen f_ψ into the policy. Only the nearest non-stationary pedestrian is considered.

Personal-space loss J_ps: a min over the horizon of |R_h + R_r − clip(d_i)|, with R_h = 0.45 m and R_r = 0.25 m, so only penetration of personal space is penalized. The full objective is J_nav + 10·J_cp + 100·J_ps.

HuRoN data-collection policy π_ρ: same architecture, trained with J_nav + 1.5·J_int, where J_int is the min predicted human-robot distance. This makes the robot seek pedestrians while still navigating toward goals.

HuRoN autonomy infrastructure: (a) a help-and-rescue module with a bumper-triggered backup maneuver (auto-recovers about 70% of simple collisions) plus remote web teleoperation; (b) AR-tag long-term anchors about 10 m apart that override the topological-node localization; (c) daily continual fine-tuning, with trajectory chaining across days via AR-tag relative poses.

setting.backbone: 8-layer CNN + FC velocity head (ExAug architecture) for the control policy, plus an MLP pedestrian-trajectory predictor; all trained from scratch (YOLOv5 + DeepSORT used only to produce training labels)
setting.training_data: HuRoN dataset (collected by the authors): 75 h and 58.7 km of autonomous robot navigation, 24 days, 5 office environments in 3 university buildings, >4000 human-robot interactions. It is split into equal interaction-enriched (w_i=1.5) and naïve (w_i=0) subsets; the main policy uses the interaction-enriched subset. The pedestrian predictor additionally uses 10,000 social-force-model simulated two-agent scenarios, mixed half-and-half with real data in each batch.
setting.observation: monocular onboard RGB (current + 5 past frames) + subgoal image from the topological graph; odometry used for training labels; spherical camera used for pedestrian detection only in training
setting.action_space: continuous linear and angular velocity (predicts 8-step horizon, executes the first command)
setting.simulator: real world only (social force model used only to synthesize predictor training data)
setting.privileged: pre-exploration: a topological graph of goal images from a prior teleoperated traversal (evaluation goal images were collected over two months earlier); AR tags used for localization during data collection

numbers_note: All results are real-robot, on the authors' own evaluation protocol; there is no standard benchmark. GR (goal arrival rate) is mapped to SR. The human-rating user study (17 subjects, 4 questions, 0–4 scale) is reported only in Fig. 7. Continual-learning intervention curves are in Fig. 10; the text reports only 0.18 interventions per 10-minute trajectory, a 95.5% reduction over day 1.
results: On 15 real-robot image-goal runs among pedestrians in 3 office environments, SACSoN trained on the interaction-enriched HuRoN data reached GR 1.000, SPL 0.888 and STL 0.692, with 1 pedestrian collision, 2 obstacle collisions and 57.609 s of personal-space violation. ExAug trained on the same data scored GR 0.800, SPL 0.692, 20 pedestrian collisions and 85.248 s PSV. SACSoN therefore cuts pedestrian collisions by over 80% and PSV by over 30%, and it was rated higher by 17 users. Interaction-seeking collection yields closer interactions (2.43 m vs 2.67 m) and a better pedestrian predictor (MSE 0.0083 vs 0.0095 with social-force data mixed in). Continual learning reduced remote interventions by 95.5% over 5 days.
limitations: Only the nearest single non-stationary pedestrian is modeled, so group and multi-pedestrian interactions are not handled; the HuRoN dataset also lacks complex group scenes.
Environments are limited to office buildings.

The evaluation is small (15 runs, pedestrians instructed to walk around the robot, 17-subject user study that is 80% students) and compares only against ExAug and a naïve-data ablation, not other social-navigation methods.
compares_to: Pedestrian predictor trained only on social-force simulation
